children: Google parent Alphabet agreed to provide additional privacy protections to salvage its $10 million acquisition of data from bankrupt Spirit Airlines.

The revised agreement, filed Monday in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court of New York, resolved objections from unions representing Spirit Airlines pilots and flight attendants who warned that personal employment files would be included to train commercial artificial intelligence systems. A bankruptcy court had previously delayed approval of Google's purchase of the data following the objections.

On Monday, Spirit filed a court document stating that Google had reached agreements with the unions to include new restrictions on what kinds of data can be used. The deal is subject to bankruptcy court approval.

Under the revised terms, the deal excludes medical files, drug or alcohol testing records, labor-related investigations, grievance and arbitration files, performance evaluations, payroll, and other employment-related materials. An independent verification agent will review the data usage to ensure compliance with the confidentiality and security requirements.
A Spirit spokesperson said the airline was pleased to resolve the labor objections over the "sale of deidentified data" as it seeks to maximize value for creditors.

Google won the bankruptcy auction in August for Spirit's digital archives, including decades of payroll, travel and recruiting files, along with about 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts and millions of additional digital items. Google has said it plans to use the data to improve its products and AI models and that personal information wouldn't be included in the purchase.

The objections from the flight attendants and pilots' unions claimed that the initial terms of the deal provided more robust privacy safeguards for consumers than they did for the employees who worked for the airline. A group of more than 120 members of Congress also sent a letter to both Spirit and Google in October demanding enhanced privacy protections for former Spirit employees.

"Worker data privacy in the age of AI has become a whole new worker's rights issue," Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, said Tuesday. "Without our union, there would have been no one to speak for workers in this fire sale of their private information. We fought and we won brand new protections."
